objects: regression function f; posterior credible band; frequentist coverage
assumptions: nonparametric regression with a Gaussian process prior
conclusion: The paper investigates when posterior credible bands provide uncertainty quantification comparable to frequentist confidence bands.
scope: Validity of bands for the regression function.
span: We are interested in the usefulness of the resulting posterior distribution for quantifying the remaining uncertainty about the function. More precisely, the posterior distribution allows to construct a credible band: a ball for the (weighted) uniform norm around the posterior mean of prescribed posterior probability. We investigate to what extent such a band has similar properties as a (frequentist) confidence band.

assumptions: a fixed true function satisfying the coverage setting
conclusion: Frequentist coverage requires L sufficiently large relative to function-class parameters whose needed inflation cannot be estimated from the data.
scope: The practical choice L = 1 is Bayesian but has no general frequentist coverage assurance.
span: For practice we recommend to use the value L = 1, since this corresponds to the true Bayesian procedure. It will be apparent from our results that frequentist coverage of a given parameter f is only ensured if L is large enough relative to parameters such as 𝜖 in Eq. 1.13. There is no way to estimate this from the data, and we can only be assured that the order of magnitude of the Bayesian band is also correct in the frequentist sense.

conclusion: In the counterexample the bands are too narrow when alpha < 1/2 and cover but are unnecessarily wide when alpha > 1/2.
scope: Counterexample to general accuracy when Holder and Fourier smoothness differ.
span: Thus the Hölder exponent can be both smaller or larger than the order of self-similarity. For α < 1/2 this will result in credible bands that are too narrow and hence give a mistaken impression of remaining uncertainty, while for α > 1/2 the credible bands will cover but be unnecessarily wide. Thus despite the positive results expressed in Theorems 1 and 2, credible bands are not necessarily accurate.
